title: Neutrality and current belong to a frame
question: How can a neutral current acquire charge density?
recap: Charge density and the current along the motion mix when the frame changes, so a wire that is neutral while it carries a current has a charge density in a frame moving along it. There is no single charge velocity to find by dividing current by charge density: in a neutral wire that ratio divides by zero.
premises: Use a physical charge-current distribution and a boost along x.
Track the same isolated body when comparing its total charge.
limitations: Charge density is not total charge.
A neutral two-species current need not have a single common velocity.

overview.text: Charge density and the current along the motion mix when the frame changes, so a wire that is neutral while it carries a current has a charge density in a frame moving along it. There is no single charge velocity to find by dividing current by charge density: in a neutral wire that ratio divides by zero.

full.spoken: The primed charge density is gamma times rho minus v times the current along x over c squared; the primed current along x is gamma times the current along x minus v times rho.

full.text: The current components across the motion, \(J_y\) and \(J_z\), are unchanged. For a neutral wire, \(\rho = 0\), carrying current \(J_x\), the new density is \(\rho' = -\gamma vJ_x/c^2\), which is not zero for any \(v \ne 0\). To see why, transform each kind of charge on its own: the positive ions and the moving electrons have different velocities, so their densities change by different factors.

Charge is conserved in every frame: density and current together obey the continuity equation. The total charge of one body is the same in both frames when each frame adds up the charge at one of its own instants. A fixed box of space is a different comparison, because charge flows through its walls. The charge-and-current laboratory compares the densities and the total charge of a body.

full.returnCaption: Return to how a neutral wire carries charge density in another frame.

items: Write down the charge density \(\rho\) and all three current components.
Transform \(\rho\) and \(J_x\) together, as a pair: \(\rho' = \gamma(\rho - vJ_x/c^2)\) and \(J'_x = \gamma(J_x - v\rho)\).
Leave \(J_y\) and \(J_z\) unchanged, since they are across the motion.
If the wire is neutral, do not divide \(J_x\) by \(\rho\). To find a velocity, transform the positive and the negative charges separately.
Check the continuity equation, and compare the total charge of the same body, before comparing totals between frames.

margin.text: Einstein treats convection current, charge carried along by moving bodies, and this edition keeps his account as he gives it instead of turning it into a general formula for a single charged fluid. The four-current, which combines \(\rho\) and \(J\) into one four-vector, came later; it is used here only to check results.
